claims.text: The target coatings have nanoscale FCC/BCC layers, typically 5–50 nm thick.
Progressive plastic deformation under sustained moderate-to-high stress and temperature is governed by interface-associated, dislocation-dominated creep acting in synergy with short-range order.
Interfaces are preferential sites for dislocation nucleation.
Short-range order modulates dislocation emission.
Short-range order changes the rate of dislocation cross-slip.
Short-range order creates local barriers that pin or impede dislocation glide.
Short-range order can also locally facilitate dislocation movement.
Short-range order delays or partially suppresses diffusion-based flow.
Beyond a critical temperature or stress, the creep mechanism partially shifts toward diffusion.
The high-temperature or high-stress diffusion occurs preferentially along interfaces and grain boundaries.
The onset of enhanced diffusion produces a notable increase in steady-state creep rate.
Dislocation-based creep remains stable as stress or temperature rises until the critical point is reached.
Short-range order makes the onset of creep acceleration more gradual than in simpler, non-entropic multilayers.
Conventional metallic multilayers exhibit more abrupt transitions to diffusion-dominated creep.
Conventional metallic multilayers have lower tolerance for sustained loads because they have fewer barriers to slip and less stable interfaces.
The proposed mechanism applies only while nanoscale layer thickness and moderate short-range order are maintained.
Large-scale coarsening or loss of interfaces can invalidate the proposed mechanism.
Appropriate aging can produce pronounced short-range order, whereas rapid quenching can deliberately minimize it.
The proposed tests span near-ambient temperature to 700 K and sustained loads of 0.5–3.0 GPa.
Identical creep behavior, dislocation nucleation, and diffusion signatures in high-SRO and low-SRO multilayers would falsify the claim that SRO is the dominant governing factor.
